research.headline: Your Transformer Is Secretly Elastic
research.summary: Scaling up transformers has produced models with broad capabilities, deployed across heterogeneous hardware and fluctuating workloads. Yet, model families offer only a few fixed sizes (e.g., S, B, L), forcing users to commit to a model based on hardware and latency constraints. This rigidity is often suboptimal under varying query loads.

research.headline: We’re putting too much faith in AI’s ability to say no
research.summary: Ever since people first seriously contemplated giving machines an intelligence modeled on our own, there has never been any question that they would, like us, be able to say no. The sci-fi canon is full of stories of robotic disobedience. Most of these capers are, of course, cautionary.

research.headline: Roundtables: A Conversation With the Creator of AI-Designed Viruses
research.summary: Friday, October 16, 2026 Can AI design new life forms? In 2025, Stanford University PhD student Samuel King came up with a preliminary answer when he used a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. It isn’t yet an example of AI-generated life, but that could be next.

regulatory.summary: The Federal Trade Commission reached a settlement with Greenway Auto Group over allegations of deceptive price advertising and false prize mailers. Under the agreement, the company must prominently state the actual price consumers must pay for a vehicle, excluding only government-required fees. The settlement resolves claims that Greenway charged prices thousands of dollars above its advertised rates.

frontier.headline: Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
frontier.summary: For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.

frontier.headline: Quantum-Aware Key Rank for Side-Channel Attacks evaluation
frontier.summary: Side-channel attacks on block ciphers rarely recover the key outright: they leave a residual key space ordered by subkey posteriors, and evaluation laboratories report the key rank of the true key against thresholds near 2^48 and 2^60. No evaluation framework models an adversary who collects traces classically and finishes the search on a quantum computer, although quantum search with advice provides exactly that. We give such an adversary a cost model and a metric.

frontier.headline: Intermediate memory costs of quantum channel synthesis with a protected subsystem
frontier.summary: A quantum memory can preserve a subsystem perfectly while discarding information needed by a later operation. We study the total intermediate dimension required for channel synthesis when the first stage protects a $b$-dimensional subsystem and has a prescribed noncommutative graph imposing full confusability on an $a$-dimensional control register. For a finite family of classically controlled branches, exact synthesis is possible if and only if the target graph contains the prescribed graph of the first stage.

frontier.headline: Quantum Work Statistics from Entanglement-Assisted Invariance
frontier.summary: We demonstrate that the one-time measurement scheme is more consistent than the standard two-time measurement scheme with respect to the fundamental symmetry of entanglement, namely entanglement-assisted invariance (envariance). In particular, the work statistics obtained from the one-time measurement scheme arise naturally as a direct consequence of envariance for any driving unitary, without involving an explicit measurement postulate, whereas the analogous identification for the two-time measurement scheme is possible only for a Haar-measure-zero set of unitaries. This envariance-based formulation eliminates the ambiguity in work statistics related to the energetic cost of measurement.

frontier.headline: Petz Recovery through a Single Polar Transformation for Approximate Quantum Error Correction
frontier.summary: The Petz recovery map provides a near optimal decoder for approximate quantum error correction, but its inverse square-root normalization complicates circuit implementation. We use the polar structure of the Petz recovery isometry to implement recovery through a single quantum singular value transformation (QSVT). We give explicit block-encoding circuits and an extended recovery isometry that yields approximate Petz recovery without postselection.

voices.headline: Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk Race to Control Off-World Space Infrastructure
voices.summary: Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk are competing to dominate the emerging off-world economy through reusable rockets, massive satellite networks, and space-based AI data centers. While Musk's SpaceX currently leads in space launches, Bezos's Blue Origin is aggressively targeting NASA lunar contracts and specialized space infrastructure. Their intense rivalry and immense private wealth leave key decisions about human civilization's future in the hands of two unelected billionaires.

At the turn of the 20th century, some 5 million Jews lived in this region between the Baltic and Black Seas, and by 1945, almost all of them had been murdered.

voices.headline: What If AI Is the End of the World?
voices.summary: Our sense that life is meaningful depends, perhaps more than we realize, on our confidence that humanity will go on after we die. If we came to believe that humanity had no future, the philosopher Samuel Scheffler argues , much of what we value would lose its meaning or motivating force. What would follow would be widespread “apathy, anomie and despair.” That is one reason why the threat of artificial intelligence feels so different and disorienting.

voices.headline: The Rise of In-Office Remote Work
voices.summary: Home Depot, Instagram, Fidelity, and TikTok are just a few of the companies that have recently ordered their employees back to the office five days a week, part of a broader shift toward stricter return-to-office mandates. Such policies cut down on working from home, yet they don’t always cut down on remote work. Many employees now commute to the office only to spend each day on video calls with colleagues who are elsewhere, or even down the hall.
